strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: closing the performance gap between memory-efficient target-free methods and target-based methods, which is relevant given the trend toward scaling Q-networks.

The proposed method (iS-QN) is simple, elegant, and easy to implement as a modification to DQN/CQL, requiring only a small increase in parameters (extra linear heads) rather than doubling network size.
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings: online and offline RL, two architectures (CNN and IMPALA), with and without LayerNorm, and both DQN and CQL, showing consistent trends.
Good use of rigorous statistical practices (IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, AUC as primary metric) following Agarwal et al. 2021 recommendations.

Provides mechanistic insight into why the method works via gradient cosine similarity analysis and effective rank (srank) of representations, which helps explain rather than just demonstrate the improvement.
The ablation with Ensemble Shared Features (ES-CQL) supports the generality of the 'shared linear head' idea beyond the iterated Q-learning framing.
The paper is well-written and clearly positioned relative to a large body of related work on target-network alternatives and regularization techniques.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to discrete-action Atari (DQN/CQL); no continuous-control experiments are included despite the method's clear motivation for large actor-critic networks (e.g., CrossQ-like settings) — the authors even mention continuous action spaces as future work, leaving a significant application area for target-free methods untested.

The number of Atari games is fairly small (15, further reduced to 10 for IMPALA and offline experiments) for AUC-based conclusions, and choice of K (number of heads) appears to require environment/architecture-specific tuning (K=49 hurts for CNN but helps for IMPALA), suggesting sensitivity that isn't fully characterized.

No wall-clock/compute overhead analysis is given beyond a qualitative claim of 'comparable training time'; given the loss sums over K Bellman terms and stores K+1 heads, some quantitative compute comparison would strengthen the memory-vs-compute tradeoff argument.

The head architecture only replaces the last linear layer; it's unclear how sensitive results are to using more than one shared layer as target vs. only the head, i.e. there's limited ablation on how much of the network should be shared versus separate.

Some claims (e.g., 'iS-DQN K=9 outperforms target-based approach by 6%') are based on a single run of AUC comparison with fairly wide/overlapping confidence intervals in places (e.g., Figure 3 left, K=49 box overlaps with TB-DQN), and statistical significance of the improvement over TB is not clearly established.

The paper does not compare against other lightweight alternatives to a full target network (e.g., Polyak averaging with different rates, EMA of only certain layers) which could serve as simpler baselines achieving similar memory savings.

The related regularization techniques (e.g., CrossQ/BatchNorm) are shown to underperform in the discrete setting but this is based on limited games (Figure 12 right, only 5 games), which weakens the strength of this comparison.

strengths: The core idea is simple, elegant, and cheap to implement: sharing feature parameters between online and target networks while keeping only a frozen linear head as the 'target', combined with iterated Q-learning heads, is a clever way to reduce memory footprint while retaining stability benefits of target networks.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a diverse set of settings: online Atari (CNN and IMPALA architectures), offline Atari (CQL), continuous control (DMC Hard with SimbaV2/SAC), and even large-scale language RL (ILQL on Wordle with GPT-2), which is a broad and convincing testbed for a resource-efficiency claim.

Good use of statistically rigorous evaluation practices (IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, AUC normalization) following Agarwal et al. (2021) recommendations, and reporting per-game learning curves in the appendix for transparency.

Ablations and analyses (Section 5.5) attempting to explain why the method works—gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, target churn, and effective rank/srank analysis—add some mechanistic insight beyond pure benchmarking.
The paper reports both memory savings (parameter counts) and confirms no substantial increase in training time/FLOPs (Appendix B), directly supporting the practical resource-efficiency motivation.
The related work section is thorough and clearly positions the contribution relative to prior target-free methods, regularization techniques, and iterated Q-learning literature.
The additional Ensemble Shared Features (ES-CQL) variant shows the parameter-sharing idea generalizes beyond the specific iterated-Q-learning instantiation, strengthening the generality claim.
weaknesses: The number of heads K is an important new hyperparameter whose optimal value varies unpredictably across settings and architectures (e.g., K=9 best for CNN, K=49 better for IMPALA, K=1~K=9 similar for SAC), and no clear principled guidance or automatic selection method is given, which limits practical usability and adds tuning burden that partially offsets the claimed simplicity/efficiency advantage.

The theoretical justification is fairly thin: the paper leans heavily on empirical demonstration and post-hoc explanatory diagnostics (cosine similarity, target churn, srank) without a formal analysis of convergence or stability guarantees for the shared-feature target construction, unlike some cited prior works (e.g., Schmitt et al., 2022) that provide theoretical guarantees for related ideas.

Baseline hyperparameters are explicitly not retuned for the new architectures/algorithms ('the same hyperparameters as those provided in the original target-based approaches are used without further tuning'), which raises concern that comparisons might be somewhat unfair or that the target-free/iS-QN variants could be further improved (or the target-based baseline underperforming) with proper tuning specific to each method.

Some datasets/domains use relatively few seeds or limited numbers of tasks/games (5 seeds per Atari game with 15 or 10 games, 7 DMC tasks), and although CIs are reported, the effect sizes in several comparisons (e.g., iS-SAC K=1 vs K=9 overlapping with TB-SAC) are sometimes marginal, making some specific numerical claims (e.g., '6% improvement over target-based') less robust than presented.

The mechanism claims in Section 5.5 (e.g., 'target churn', gradient cosine similarity) are somewhat ad hoc metrics introduced specifically for this paper without independent validation or comparison to established diagnostic tools, and the causal story linking these metrics to final performance is more suggestive/correlational than rigorously established.

The paper's headline claim of 'bridging the performance gap' and sometimes 'outperforming' target-based methods (e.g., iS-DQN K=9 beating TB-DQN by 6%) could be partly attributable to the additional loss terms/heads acting as an implicit auxiliary/regularization signal rather than purely to the shared-feature trick; the paper does not fully disentangle the contribution of iterated Q-learning's auxiliary heads from the shared-feature mechanism in a controlled way (e.g., an ablation with separate non-shared iterated heads at equal head count is not clearly presented as a controlled comparison in the main text).

The paper does not report wall-clock or memory comparisons against alternative resource-efficient methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, or other streaming-only baselines like Vasan et al. 2024, Gallici et al. 2025) which are mentioned in related work but not empirically benchmarked, limiting the completeness of the 'resource-efficient RL' positioning.

Loss aggregation design choice (summing K Bellman losses) is acknowledged as ad hoc and left for future work, and the one alternative explored (discounting future terms in SAC) is applied inconsistently across experiments, suggesting the method's default recipe may not be robust/well-optimized across settings.

strengths: Introduces a simple and practical idea (sharing feature parameters between online and target networks, represented via linear heads) that meaningfully reduces the target-free vs target-based performance gap while keeping a low memory footprint.
Combines the shared-features idea with iterated Q-learning in a natural way (iS-QN), and shows this combination provides further gains beyond simply sharing features (K=1).

Extremely broad empirical validation: online discrete control (Atari, two architectures, with/without normalization), offline discrete control (CQL), continuous control (SAC/SimbaV2), language-model-based offline RL (ILQL/Wordle), and streaming RL (Stream Q(λ)) — demonstrating generality of the approach across very different algorithmic and architectural settings.

Includes thoughtful analysis of the underlying mechanism: gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, a novel 'target churn' metric, and effective rank (srank) of representations, providing some mechanistic insight into why the method works.

Extensive ablations (target update period T, number of heads K, network width, meta-learned per-head loss weighting) and additional experiments (MellowMax combination, mixed-precision training) that stress-test robustness and generality of the method.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameter tables, per-game learning curves in the appendix, code availability implied, and transparent reporting of training time/FLOPs showing the memory savings do not come from reduced compute.

Orthogonality to existing target-free regularization techniques (MellowMax, BatchNorm/LayerNorm) is explicitly demonstrated, showing the method can be layered on top of prior work rather than being mutually exclusive with it.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely stitches together two existing ideas (a shared-backbone target head and iterated Q-learning from Vincent et al. 2025b) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

The number of Bellman iterations K is an important new hyperparameter with no principled selection rule; the paper only offers a heuristic 'increase until it stops helping,' and the optimal K varies considerably across domains/architectures (e.g., K=49 helps for IMPALA but hurts for CNN), which complicates practical deployment.

Some result comparisons appear to have overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., iS-SAC K=9 said to be 'on par' with target-based approach in DMC), which slightly weakens the strength of some headline claims of closing the gap.

The reported memory savings do not translate into reduced training time or FLOPs (as the authors themselves acknowledge), limiting the practical benefit to memory-constrained settings only, which somewhat narrows the significance of the contribution.

Atari evaluations use relatively small game subsets (15 or 10 games) for computational reasons, which, combined with the many architecture/normalization variants tested, could raise concerns about the statistical robustness of some fine-grained comparisons despite the use of IQM and bootstrapped CIs.

The paper introduces many additional variants and results (Ensemble Shared Features, MellowMax combination, meta-gradient weighting, mixed precision) that, while interesting, are explored only superficially (single or few games/tasks) and mostly relegated to the appendix, diluting the focus of the main contribution.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: reducing the memory overhead of target networks while retaining their stabilizing benefits.

Very broad empirical evaluation spanning online discrete control (Atari, CNN and IMPALA backbones), offline discrete control (CQL), continuous control (SAC/SimbaV2 on DMC Hard), a language-model RL task (ILQL/Wordle with GPT-2), and a streaming RL setting -- this breadth is a genuine strength.

Useful mechanistic analysis (gradient cosine similarity to target-based updates, 'target churn', effective rank/srank) that attempts to explain why sharing features narrows the gap, going beyond a pure black-box performance comparison.

Reasonably thorough ablations on target update period T, number of heads K, and network width, plus a pilot study on mixed-precision training and an alternative 'Ensemble Shared Features' variant, showing some robustness of the core idea.
Reproducibility materials (hyperparameter tables, per-game learning curves, code availability statement) are provided in detail.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is incremental: it is essentially a straightforward combination of (a) a shared-trunk/frozen-head architecture, which is conceptually similar to existing multi-head Q-network designs (e.g., bootstrapped DQN-style heads), and (b) the already-published iterated Q-network idea (Vincent et al., 2025b), applied here mainly by removing the separate target copy and paying for K linear heads instead.

K (number of parallel Bellman updates/heads) is a new, sensitive hyperparameter whose optimal value varies substantially across domains and even across architectures within the same domain (e.g., K=49 helps with IMPALA but hurts with the plain CNN, K=9 works well in Atari but only matches K=1 in DMC). No principled selection rule is given beyond 'increase K until performance degrades,' which undermines the practical resource-efficiency claim, since tuning requires multiple runs.

The method does not reduce training time or FLOPs (explicitly acknowledged in Section 6/Appendix B), so the practical benefit is restricted to peak memory footprint; for many of the motivating use-cases (large models, edge devices) compute cost is often equally or more limiting than memory, weakening the significance of the contribution.

The 'why it works' analysis (cosine similarity, target churn, srank) is purely empirical/post-hoc and offers no theoretical guarantee or convergence analysis, in contrast to related chaining-value-function work (Schmitt et al., 2022) that provides guarantees for the linear case.

Some reported gains (e.g., iS-DQN K=9 outperforming TB-DQN by 6% AUC, or iS-ILQL beating TB-ILQL by 5%) are based on a fairly small number of seeds/games (5 seeds, 10-15 Atari games) and confidence intervals in several figures visibly overlap between iS variants and target-based baselines, so claims of 'closing' or 'surpassing' the gap should be interpreted cautiously.

The meta-gradient weighting experiment (Appendix D.4) is inconclusive -- learned coefficients converge to uniform weights, essentially showing that this added complexity does not improve over the simple static-sum loss, which is presented as a positive finding but largely just validates that the added machinery was unnecessary.

The extremely long appendix (29 pages vs. 10 main pages) suggests the core result required substantial additional experiments and qualifications to be convincing, and the paper's main text alone does not fully establish robustness of the proposed method without heavy reliance on supplementary material.
